title: Why Bitter Coffee Starts to Taste Better
summary:
Your first sip of black coffee can taste awful. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are wired to avoid. Yet millions of people grow to love that same taste. What changes? Scientists at UC San Francisco may have found an important part of the answer.

The team studied dopamine, a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward and learning. Most research has looked at fast dopamine signals that fire within seconds of something rewarding. The new study, published November 4 in Nature, looks at a slower system instead. It responds to information from inside the body, helping the brain learn about the benefits of food after it has been eaten.

When food reaches the gut, sensors detect nutrients such as sugar and fat. That information travels to the brain, where it can trigger a dopamine response that builds slowly and lasts several minutes. Senior author Zachary Knight and graduate student James Grove gave mice sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid straight into their stomachs, and watched dopamine activity across their brains.

The strongest response appeared in the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA, a brain region involved in emotion and learning. "We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," Knight said.

The team then tested whether the signal really changes food preferences. When they interrupted the pathway, mice still ate normally but could no longer learn that an unfamiliar flavor meant calories were coming. When they switched those fibers on after mice tasted a calorie-free flavor, the animals still developed a liking for it. Once the brain links coffee's taste with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better."
why_it_matters: This helps explain how our likes and dislikes are learned, not just born with us, and why foods that taste strange at first can become favourites over time.

background_read: Dopamine is a chemical messenger in the brain that helps us feel reward and learn from what happens to us.
The gut is the part of the body where food is digested, and it sends signals to the brain about what we have eaten.
Learning to like a food takes time: the brain links a flavour with how the food makes the body feel after it is eaten.
Coffee contains caffeine, a substance that makes people feel more awake, which is one reason adults often drink it.
